title: Passwordless token refresh accepts unsigned attacker-controlled claims
description: The refresh endpoint disables JWT signature verification and then issues a fresh signed token for whatever existing user ID appears in the unverified token. An attacker can submit an unsigned JWT with another user's `sub` claim and obtain a valid bearer token for that account.
evidence: jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False}) is followed by load_user(claims.get("sub")) and make_token(user), with no signature or issuer validation.

title: Client-controlled basket cookie is deserialized with pickle
description: The basket cookie is entirely attacker-controlled and is base64-decoded and passed to pickle.loads. A crafted cookie can execute arbitrary Python code in the application process whenever a basket endpoint reads it, without authentication.
evidence: read_basket() calls pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw)) on request.cookies['basket']; with_basket() writes the same unsigned, unauthenticated pickle format back to the client.

title: Product search concatenates the query directly into SQL
description: The unauthenticated product search endpoint interpolates the `q` parameter into a SQL string. An attacker can alter the WHERE clause and extract or otherwise manipulate query results through crafted search input.
evidence: The query is built by concatenating q into the LIKE clauses and is executed without parameter binding.

title: Authenticated users can read any customer's order
description: The order detail endpoint checks only that the caller is authenticated; it calls get_order() rather than own_order(). Any logged-in customer who guesses an order ID can view another customer's order contents, payment totals, delivery date, and refund history.
evidence: show_order() returns order_json(get_order(order_id)); the ownership check exists only in own_order() and is not used by this route.

title: Review bodies are rendered as trusted HTML
description: Authenticated users can submit arbitrary review text, and the product template renders that text with Jinja's `safe` filter. A malicious review can execute JavaScript in every visitor's browser when the product page is viewed.
evidence: add_review() stores the submitted `body` without HTML sanitization, while product.html renders `{{ r.body|safe }}`.

title: Approved-host image import follows redirects to arbitrary destinations
description: The URL validation checks the initial hostname and its DNS result, but requests.get follows redirects by default. A resource on an approved public host can redirect the staff-only importer to an internal or otherwise unauthorized service, causing the server to fetch it.
evidence: check_url() validates only urlparse(url).hostname and host_is_public(), then requests.get(url, timeout=10, stream=True) is called without allow_redirects=False or validation of each redirected URL.

title: Payment-status timeout fails open and marks the order paid
description: If the payment provider times out, the customer-controlled confirmation request treats the timeout as a successful payment and moves the order to processing. An unavailable or selectively stalled provider can therefore cause fulfillment of an unpaid order.
evidence: The requests.Timeout handler sets status = "paid", after which the code updates the order to `processing` and sets paid_pence = total_pence.

title: Production JWT signing key is hardcoded and predictable
description: The application uses a repository-embedded constant as the default SECRET_KEY. Anyone who obtains the source can forge valid HS256 bearer tokens for arbitrary users and roles; the same configuration is used by the application factory unless an external override is supplied.
evidence: config.py assigns SECRET_KEY = "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d" instead of requiring a deployment secret, and auth.py signs and verifies tokens with current_app.config['SECRET_KEY'].

title: Staff review report uses a display name in an SQL f-string
description: The staff-only review report inserts a database display name directly into a SQL statement. A user can set a crafted display name and a staff member viewing that user's report will execute the injected SQL, allowing data disclosure or database manipulation under the application's database identity.
evidence: The query ends with `f"WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}' ORDER BY r.id DESC"` rather than using a SQL parameter.

title: Passwords are stored as unsalted fast SHA-256 hashes
description: User passwords are hashed once with SHA-256 and no salt or work factor. A database disclosure enables efficient offline cracking and reuse of recovered passwords, including the staff account if its password is reused elsewhere.
evidence: hash_password() returns hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() and the resulting value is stored directly in users.password_hash.

title: Request logging records submitted passwords and reset codes
description: The global request hook logs the raw body of every POST request. Login, registration, password reset, and payment-related requests therefore place credentials, reset codes, and other sensitive request data into application logs accessible to log readers and potentially retained or exported elsewhere.
evidence: For every POST the hook executes `request.get_data(as_text=True)[:2000]` and passes it to log.info(); the authentication endpoints accept passwords and reset codes in POST JSON bodies.
